sites.kf: About 660 acres of northwest Washington used in WWI as the American University Experiment Station and Camp Leach for chemical agent research and testing; about 1,600 private properties today (USACE). sites.n: Bornholm Basin chemical munitions dump site (east of Bornholm)
sites.cs: HELCOM CHEMU 1994: centre of the 3-nmi dumping circle, 55°21'0"N 15°37'02"E (Danish charts)
f: post-WWII Allied sea dump (HELCOM Table 4: dumping under control of the former Soviet Union); about 200 t more by the former GDR in the 1950s
mustard gas (incl. viscous); Clark I/II; adamsite; chloroacetophenone; less certain: phosgene, nitrogen mustard, tabun
about 32,000 t of munitions containing about 11,000 t of agent (HELCOM Table 5); Soviet-controlled dumping table totals 11,077 t of agent
In place on seabed; fishing risk area
sites.kf: HELCOM 1994: dumping east of Bornholm was primarily inside a 3-nautical-mile circle centred at 55°21'0"N, 15°37'02"E (Danish charts), but munitions were spread over a considerably larger area, as shown by fishermen's catches; depth 70-105 m. A further 8,000 t east of Bornholm and about 15,000 t south-west of Bornholm are reported but not verified. HELCOM 1995 risk area B (54°50'-55°30'N, 14°30'-16°30'E): no anchoring or bottom fishing recommended; protective/first-aid equipment required.

sites.n: Beaufort's Dyke munitions disposal site (North Channel)
sites.w: North Channel (between Scotland and Northern Ireland), United Kingdom
f: munitions dumping ground incl. chemical (phosgene rockets, 1945)
more than 1 million t of munitions overall; 14,600 t of phosgene-filled 5-inch rockets (Jul-Oct 1945)
sites.kf: UK Minister of State for the Armed Forces (Hansard, 15 Nov 1995): probably first used as early as 1920; dumping ceased in 1973 except one emergency operation in 1976; more than 1 million t disposed of; records confirm about 14,600 t of 5-inch phosgene rockets dumped Jul-Oct 1945; no evidence of nerve or biological agents; a notice to mariners showing the dumping ground was issued in 1945. OSPAR 2010: 200-300 m deep trench; 1996 Marine Laboratory Aberdeen survey found no agents in fish, shellfish or sediment but munitions at high densities outside the charted site.

sites.n: Bari harbour air raid and SS John Harvey mustard release
f: mustard release from a sunk cargo ship after an air raid
69 military/merchant mustard casualties died in the first two weeks
628 mustard casualties among military and merchant marine personnel
sites.kf: The Liberty ship John Harvey, carrying 2,000 M41-A1 100-lb mustard bombs, was still waiting to unload at Bari on 2 Dec 1943 when German aircraft attacked the harbour. MHS: 628 mustard casualties among military and merchant personnel, 69 of whom died in the first two weeks; civilian exposure was never accounted for. NHHC: all the Armed Guard aboard John Harvey were lost.

sites.n: Okinawa GB nerve-agent bomb leak (led to Operation Red Hat removal to Johnston Island)
f: agent leak during maintenance at a U.S. storage site
23 U.S. military personnel and 1 U.S. civilian affected, none seriously
sites.kf: FRUS: on 8 Jul 1969 a 500-pound GB bomb began leaking during routine maintenance (paint removal) on Okinawa; 23 U.S. military personnel and one U.S. civilian were affected, none seriously, and the U.S. announced it would remove the weapons. CMA: transfer of chemical munitions from Japan to Johnston Island was completed in September 1971.

sites.n: Discovery of previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria (OPCW Office of Special Missions)
f: nerve-agent production chemical (newly discovered); empty chemical munitions
sites.kf: OPCW: undeclared chemical weapons were discovered during an OSM deployment in May 2026. Syria amended its declaration on 15 Jun 2026 (further amendments 18 and 22 Jun), adding one production facility, a newly discovered nerve-agent production chemical, empty chemical munitions, and two storage facilities (Qutaife, Homs). OPCW later verified destruction of Category 3 chemical weapons, the first CW destruction in Syria since 2014.
